name: Antarctica
scope: The frozen continent at the bottom of the world — the flagship keystone of this sub-strand. T1: Antarctica holds about 90% of ALL the ice on Earth, and locked in that ice is more than 70% of the planet's fresh water (invert the wonder: a single frozen continent is Earth's biggest freshwater store — the answer is Antarctica). T1/T2: despite all that ice, Antarctica is the world's largest DESERT — the dry interior gets less snowfall than the Sahara gets rain. T2: the coldest natural temperature ever reliably recorded on Earth, -89.2 C (-128.6 F), was measured at Vostok Station on the high plateau on 21 July 1983 (WMO-confirmed). T2/T3: no country owns Antarctica and it has NO permanent residents — the 1959 Antarctic Treaty set the whole continent aside for peace and science (answer = 'no one owns it / reserved for science', a defining place-fact, not a bare date). T3: the McMurdo Dry Valleys are the largest ice-free area on the continent, so cold and dry that no rain or snow has fallen for nearly 2 million years — NASA tests Mars rovers there. T3: Blood Falls pours a blood-red stream from the snout of Taylor Glacier, colored not by blood but by iron-rich brine sealed under the ice for ~2 million years (teach: it's rust from ancient trapped brine). T3/T4: the ice is up to nearly 3 miles (~4.8 km) thick. T4: sealed under ~4 km of ice sits Lake Vostok, a liquid lake the size of Lake Ontario, cut off from sunlight for perhaps 15 million years. T4: Mount Erebus on Ross Island is the southernmost active volcano on Earth and holds a rare permanent lava lake churning since at least the early 1970s (fire inside the ice). T5: katabatic winds — dense cold air sliding off the high plateau under gravity — funnel through coastal valleys at up to ~300 km/h, the strongest sustained surface winds on Earth (teach term: katabatic). T5: the ice is so heavy it has pushed Antarctica's bedrock hundreds of meters DOWN, much of it below sea level; lift the ice and the land would slowly rebound (isostasy). T5: fossil forests over 260 million years old show Antarctica was once a green corner of the supercontinent Gondwana — trees grew here in the polar twilight (deep-time payoff).
source: Grokipedia: Antarctica (primary per pipeline; automated fetch returned 403, corroborated below). Wikipedia: Antarctica; Vostok Station; Climate of Antarctica; Lake Vostok; Mount Erebus; McMurdo Dry Valleys; Blood Falls; Katabatic wind. Britannica: Antarctica/Climate; 'Coldest temperature ever recorded'. British Antarctic Survey Antarctic factsheet. WMO (-89.2 C, Vostok, 21 Jul 1983). ScienceDaily / National Geographic: Antarctic Gondwana fossil forests (>260 Ma).
framing_note: Scene-led PLACE ladder: every rung's answer is a concrete fact about THIS continent, and a distractor set of adjacent real superlatives (Greenland's ice, the Sahara's heat, the Arctic's sea ice, Death Valley) keeps all four live. Never 'What is the coldest place?' — lead with the scene and let the player KNOW the answer. Accuracy rail: Blood Falls is iron-oxide brine, not blood, and the -89.2 C record is the reliably-measured surface value (satellite readings of ~-93 C are a separate, lower figure — do not conflate). Dinner-test payoff rung: Lake Vostok sealed for 15 million years under 4 km of ice, tied with Mount Erebus's lava lake (fire under the ice) and the Gondwana fossil forests. Lane border: the 'no residents / Antarctic Treaty' rung is a place-governance fact, not a human-name/date answer — keep the answer the arrangement, not a signatory.

name: The Arctic Ocean & the North Pole
scope: The sea at the top of the world — the mirror-image pole to Antarctica. T1: the Arctic Ocean is the world's SMALLEST and SHALLOWEST ocean, ringed almost all the way around by land (Eurasia and North America) so it is nearly enclosed (invert: an ocean you could almost walk around — the answer is the Arctic). T2: stand exactly on the North Pole and there is NO LAND beneath you — only a raft of drifting sea ice floating over ~4 km of water, unlike the South Pole which sits on solid continent (the dinner-test contrast). T2/T3: the Bering Strait is the ocean's only narrow Pacific gateway, ~82 km wide — and in the Ice Age it was dry land, 'Beringia', a grassland bridge animals and people could walk across from Asia to America (teach: land bridge; answer = Beringia / the Bering land bridge, a place). T3: Arctic sea ice 'breathes' with the seasons — it grows to cover nearly the whole ocean in winter and shrinks back each summer; and sea ice is frozen SEAWATER (its salt squeezed out), a different thing from a freshwater iceberg (teach the distinction). T4: at the Pole the sun rises and sets essentially ONCE a year — about six months of daylight (midnight sun) then six months of dark (polar night). T4/T5: an undersea mountain range, the Lomonosov Ridge, runs right across the Arctic seafloor, splitting the deep basin in two — and nations argue over who owns it because it may decide the seabed border (teach: submarine ridge). T5: the Transpolar Drift is a current of moving ice that carries anything frozen into it — a stranded ship, a message bottle, spilled cargo — clear across the whole ocean from Siberia to the Atlantic over several years.
source: Grokipedia: Arctic Ocean; North Pole (primary per pipeline). Wikipedia: Arctic Ocean; North Pole; Lomonosov Ridge; Beringia; Transpolar Drift Stream; Sea ice. Britannica: Arctic Ocean; Lomonosov Ridge. WorldAtlas: smallest ocean.
framing_note: PLACE ladder anchored to the ocean itself; distractors are the other four oceans and real Arctic features (Bering Strait vs. Davis Strait, Lomonosov vs. Gakkel Ridge). Accuracy rail: the North-Pole-on-drifting-sea-ice vs. South-Pole-on-land contrast is the load-bearing correct fact — the geographic North Pole is water, not buildable land. Dinner-test payoff: the North Pole floats (there is no land under your feet). Teach sea-ice-vs-iceberg (frozen seawater vs. freshwater glacier ice) before the icebergs ladder relies on it. Lane border: the Beringia rung answers with the PLACE (the land bridge), not with the migration story — that peopling-of-the-Americas narrative is the history bank's; a one-clause mention is fine.
history_overlap: History bank may own the peopling-of-the-Americas / Beringia-migration episode as a human story; here the Beringia rung's ANSWER is the geographic land bridge itself, so keep it place-anchored and let history carry the migration narrative.

name: The Greenland ice sheet
scope: The Northern Hemisphere's great ice cap — a flagship polar wonder. T1: Greenland is the world's LARGEST island (Australia is a continent, so it doesn't count), and a single ice sheet buries about 80% of it. T1/T2: that ice is up to ~3 km thick, and its summit plateau tops 3,200 m — a high, frozen desert where research camps sit on 3 km of ice. T2: the ice is SO heavy it has pressed the middle of the island down into a bowl — much of Greenland's bedrock now lies BELOW sea level (dinner-test candidate: Greenland is bowl-shaped under the ice). T2/T3: it is the second-largest ice mass on Earth after Antarctica; if it all melted, global sea level would rise about 7 meters (24 ft). T3: hidden under the ice runs a canyon longer than any on Earth's surface — a buried 'Grand Canyon' more than 750 km (466 mi) long, carved by an ancient river before the ice came (dinner-test candidate). T3/T4: ice cores drilled from the sheet hold annual layers like tree rings — a frozen diary of more than 100,000 years of climate, and the trapped air bubbles are actual samples of ancient atmosphere (teach: ice core). T4: radar found a 31-km-wide crater buried under Hiawatha Glacier — likely an ancient meteorite impact hidden by the ice (label DISPUTED: the impact date is debated). T4: the Jakobshavn (Ilulissat) Glacier is one of the fastest-moving glaciers on Earth and Greenland's biggest iceberg factory — the berg that likely sank the Titanic calved from near here. T4/T5: in summer, meltwater braids into brilliant blue rivers across the ice and pours down vertical shafts called moulins straight to the bedrock far below (teach: moulin). T5: warm ocean water, not just warm air, eats Greenland's glaciers from BELOW — the sea undercuts the ice fronts where they meet the fjords (teach: ocean-driven melt).
source: Grokipedia: Greenland ice sheet (primary per pipeline). Wikipedia: Greenland ice sheet; Megacanyon (Greenland Grand Canyon); Hiawatha Glacier crater; Jakobshavn Glacier; Ilulissat Icefjord; Moulin (geomorphology). NASA Science / SVS: 'Greenland's Mega-Canyon' (>750 km) and 'Hidden Greenland Canyons Mean More Sea Level Rise'.
framing_note: PLACE ladder; distractors are Antarctica, other ice caps, and real Greenland features (Ilulissat vs. Petermann, Hiawatha vs. Chicxulub). Accuracy rail: 'largest island' requires teaching the island-vs-continent line (Australia is a continent), and the Hiawatha crater's impact age is genuinely DISPUTED — label it, don't state it as settled. Dinner-test payoffs: Greenland is bowl-shaped below sea level under its own ice, and there's a river-canyon longer than any surface canyon hidden beneath it. Lane border: the Titanic-berg mention is a one-rung link to the icebergs ladder — keep this rung's answer the Greenland glacier's origin, not the shipwreck.

name: Vatnajokull, Iceland
scope: Iceland's great ice cap, where fire sits under ice. T1: Vatnajokull is the largest glacier in Europe, a single ice cap covering about 8% of ALL of Iceland (~7,700 km2). T2: each winter, meltwater carves shimmering blue 'crystal ice caves' underneath the glacier — walkable only in the cold months and gone again by spring (dinner-test candidate: the blue ice caves). T2/T3: beneath the ice sit ACTIVE volcanoes, because Iceland straddles the Mid-Atlantic Ridge where the North American and Eurasian plates pull apart — so here fire literally sits under ice (teach: a spreading plate boundary). T3: Grimsvotn, buried under the ice cap, is Iceland's most active volcano, erupting every few years. T3/T4: when a volcano erupts under the ice it melts a hidden lake that suddenly bursts out in a glacial flood called a jokulhlaup — the 1996 Grimsvotn flood released about 3 km3 of water and tore bridges off the coastal ring road (teach term: jokulhlaup; dinner-test payoff). T4: at the glacier's edge, Jokulsarlon is a lagoon full of icebergs calved from an outlet glacier; they drift to the sea and wash back onto black sand as 'Diamond Beach'. T5: eruptions trapped UNDER a glacier build flat-topped 'table mountains' called tuyas — Iceland's odd steep-sided flat mesas were each born by fire beneath the ice (teach: tuya).
source: Grokipedia: Vatnajokull; Grimsvotn (primary per pipeline). Wikipedia: Vatnajokull; Grimsvotn; Jokulhlaup; Jokulsarlon; Tuya; Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Global Volcanism Program (Smithsonian): Grimsvotn. Vatnajokull National Park (official).
framing_note: PLACE ladder; distractors are other Icelandic and European glaciers/volcanoes (Langjokull, Eyjafjallajokull, Hekla, the Alps' Aletsch). Accuracy rail: 'largest glacier in Europe' is true by area and by the usual continental framing, but note the Novaya Zemlya (Severny Island) ice cap is sometimes cited as larger by volume depending on where Europe's edge is drawn — frame as 'Europe's largest glacier' without over-claiming a volume record. Dinner-test payoffs: the winter-only blue ice caves and the jokulhlaup (a volcano melts a hidden lake that bursts out under the ice). Teach jokulhlaup and tuya before testing them. Lane border: none — the volcano and plate-tectonics content is squarely geography; no food-origin rung.

name: Perito Moreno Glacier, Patagonia
scope: The calving glacier of Argentine Patagonia. T1: the Perito Moreno Glacier ends in a wall of ice about 5 km wide and ~70 m tall (240 ft) rising straight out of a lake — and every few minutes a chunk cracks off and crashes into the water (hook: the calving wall). T2: for about 80 years (mid-1940s to the 2010s) Perito Moreno was famous as one of the FEW glaciers on Earth that wasn't shrinking — it stayed almost exactly in balance while others retreated (the 'balanced glacier'; honest note that it has recently begun to retreat). T2/T3: the glacier flows forward until it TOUCHES the far shore and dams an arm of Lake Argentino; with no outlet, the trapped water rises up to ~30 m higher on one side (teach: an ice dam). T3/T4: pressure slowly tunnels through the ice and carves a great ARCH — an ice bridge — that finally, spectacularly, collapses in a 'rupture' event crowds gather to watch (dinner-test payoff: the rupture of the ice bridge). T4/T5: Perito Moreno is only one of ~48 glaciers pouring off the Southern Patagonian Ice Field — the largest ice mass outside the poles that you can reach on foot, and the third-biggest freshwater store on Earth after Antarctica and Greenland.
source: Grokipedia: Perito Moreno Glacier (primary per pipeline). Wikipedia: Perito Moreno Glacier; Southern Patagonian Ice Field; Lago Argentino; Los Glaciares National Park. Quasar / Calafate Tours travel guides (rupture-cycle mechanics, corroborated).
framing_note: PLACE ladder; distractors are other named glaciers and Patagonian features (Upsala, Viedma, the Grey Glacier, the Northern vs. Southern Ice Field). Accuracy rail: state the 'wasn't retreating' fame in the past tense with the honest recent-retreat note — do NOT present Perito Moreno as permanently stable. Dinner-test payoff: the ice-bridge rupture (the glacier dams a lake, water rises 30 m, then the ice arch collapses). Lane border: none.

name: Svalbard & the Global Seed Vault
scope: The Arctic archipelago that guards the world's crops. T1: on a frozen mountainside near Longyearbyen in Norway's Svalbard islands, a lone doorway leads into the Global Seed Vault — a 'doomsday' backup library holding seeds from almost every country on Earth (answer = the Svalbard Global Seed Vault). T2: the seeds sit ~100+ m inside the mountain, kept frozen by the surrounding PERMAFROST so they would stay cold even if the power failed — that's WHY this frozen place was chosen (teach: permafrost as a natural freezer). T2/T3: the vault can hold about 4.5 million seed samples as a backup for the world's other seed banks — and it has already done its job once: seeds were withdrawn to rebuild a collection destroyed by the war in Syria (dinner-test payoff: the vault's first real withdrawal). T3/T4: in 2017 an unusually warm winter thawed some permafrost and meltwater seeped into the entrance tunnel — it froze before reaching the seeds, which were never harmed, but it was a warning, and the tunnel has since been waterproofed (accuracy rail: the seeds were safe). T4: Svalbard is one of the northernmost inhabited places on Earth — Longyearbyen sits at about 78 N, and by old local advice you carry a rifle outside town because of polar bears. T5: Longyearbyen is so far north the sun doesn't set for ~4 months in summer and doesn't rise for ~4 months in winter — and by local rule you can't be buried in town, because bodies won't decompose in the permafrost (dinner-test candidate).
source: Grokipedia: Svalbard Global Seed Vault; Longyearbyen (primary per pipeline). Wikipedia: Svalbard Global Seed Vault; Longyearbyen; Svalbard. Snopes / GRID-Arendal / Weather Channel (2017 tunnel-flood fact-check, corroborated); Crop Trust (official, capacity & Syria withdrawal).
framing_note: PLACE ladder; distractors are other Arctic settlements and facilities (Ny-Alesund, Barentsburg, the Arctic World Archive, Fort Knox as a red-herring 'vault'). Accuracy rail: the 2017 event flooded only the ACCESS TUNNEL and the seeds were never at risk — do not let a rung imply the collection was damaged. Dinner-test payoffs: the vault has actually been used once (the Syria withdrawal), and the 'no burials in Longyearbyen' permafrost fact. Lane border: the polar bear appears as context for the rifle rule — keep that rung's answer the PLACE/rule (northernmost town, carry a rifle), NOT the bear's biology, which is the animal bank's.

name: Permafrost & Siberia's frozen ground
scope: The permanently frozen earth of the far north, anchored to real Siberian places. T1: across northern Siberia, Canada, and Alaska the ground stays frozen solid all year round — 'permafrost' — locking up roughly a QUARTER of the Northern Hemisphere's land in ice-cemented soil (teach: permafrost = ground frozen 2+ years straight). T2: that frozen ground is a natural freezer for the deep past — in Siberia's permafrost scientists dig out Ice Age mammoths so well-preserved they still have fur, skin, and food in their stomachs (the PLACE preserves them). T2/T3: in the Sakha Republic, the Batagaika crater — nicknamed the 'gateway to the underworld' — is the world's biggest permafrost slump: a 1-km-long gash up to 100 m deep that has been growing ~30 m a year since the ground began thawing (dinner-test payoff; teach: megaslump / thermokarst). T3/T4: permafrost holds huge amounts of frozen methane and ancient carbon, and as it thaws it releases greenhouse gas — Batagaika's exposed walls reveal soil layers up to ~650,000 years old, a window into deep time AND a carbon store. T4: on the Yamal Peninsula, thawing permafrost has let underground gas build up and BLOW OUT, leaving mysterious near-perfect round craters tens of meters across, first spotted in 2014 (dinner-test candidate; teach: gas-blowout crater). T5: in a Siberian experiment called Pleistocene Park, scientists herd grazing animals to trample the snow and keep the ground colder, testing whether a restored grassland could slow the permafrost thaw.
source: Grokipedia: Permafrost; Batagaika crater (primary per pipeline). Wikipedia: Permafrost; Batagaika crater; Yamal Peninsula craters; Pleistocene Park. NASA Earth Observatory ('Batagaika Crater Expands'); USGS EROS; Live Science ('gateway to the underworld' megaslump).
framing_note: PLACE/theme ladder anchored to named Siberian sites; distractors are other Arctic landforms and real craters (a pingo, a thermokarst lake, the Yamal crater vs. Batagaika, a meteorite crater). Accuracy rail: the Yamal craters are gas-blowout features from thawing permafrost, NOT meteorite or sinkhole craters — teach the mechanism. Dinner-test payoffs: the Batagaika megaslump ('gateway to the underworld') and the exploding Yamal gas craters. Lane border: the mammoth is an EXTINCT ANIMAL owned by the animal bank — keep the mammoth rung's answer the PLACE-fact (the frozen ground preserves the carcass), never the mammoth's anatomy or behavior.

name: Icebergs: how they calve and drift
scope: The wandering ice of the sea, with the Titanic's berg at its heart. T1: when you see an iceberg at sea, only about a TENTH of it shows above the water — the dangerous bulk hides below ('tip of the iceberg'; invert: the huge hidden mass is the hook, '~90% is underwater' the answer). T2: an iceberg is FRESH water, not seawater — it 'calves' (breaks off) from the end of a glacier or ice sheet, which is packed-down snow, then floats away (teach: calving; iceberg vs. sea ice). T2/T3: off Newfoundland lies 'Iceberg Alley', where bergs born on Greenland's glaciers ride the cold Labrador Current south into shipping lanes — the berg that sank the Titanic in 1912 drifted down this way from Greenland (dinner-test payoff: the Titanic's berg came from Greenland). T3/T4: after the Titanic, nations founded the International Ice Patrol, which still tracks the ~1,000 icebergs a year that drift south of the shipping lanes so ships can steer clear. T4: the BIGGEST icebergs come from Antarctica, not the Arctic — flat-topped 'tabular' bergs calve off floating ice shelves, and A23a, one of the largest ever, is bigger than some whole countries (dinner-test candidate; teach: tabular berg vs. ice shelf). T5: really old, dense glacier ice can glow deep blue or even green — thousands of years of pressure have squeezed the air bubbles out, so it absorbs every color but blue (teach: why some bergs are blue).
source: Grokipedia: Iceberg (primary per pipeline). Wikipedia: Iceberg; Iceberg that sank the Titanic; Iceberg B-15 / A23a; International Ice Patrol. NOAA / US Coast Guard Navigation Center (International Ice Patrol). National Geographic Education (iceberg formation).
framing_note: PLACE/process ladder; distractors are real ocean features and place-facts (Iceberg Alley vs. the Grand Banks, sea ice vs. iceberg, Arctic vs. Antarctic berg shapes). Accuracy rail: an iceberg is freshwater glacier ice that CALVED off land ice — distinct from sea ice (frozen seawater); the '~90% below water' figure comes from the ice-vs-seawater density ratio, so keep it as ~90%, not a made-up exact number. Dinner-test payoffs: the Titanic's berg drifted down from Greenland via Iceberg Alley, and Antarctic tabular bergs bigger than a country. Lane border: the Titanic SHIPWRECK narrative belongs to the history bank; here every answer is iceberg geography/origin/optics, not the sinking's human story.
history_overlap: History bank may own the Titanic disaster as a human episode; this ladder's answers are the iceberg's ORIGIN, drift route (Iceberg Alley), and physics (freshwater, 90% submerged, blue ice) — keep the shipwreck as one-clause context only.

name: The Great Aletsch Glacier, Swiss Alps
scope: Europe's mightiest mountain glacier — a temperate, alpine counterpoint to the polar ice. T1: the Great Aletsch Glacier in Switzerland is the largest and longest glacier in the ALPS — a river of ice about 23 km long (roughly 20 km today) holding on the order of 10 billion tonnes of ice (hook: a glacier you can watch from the peaks above). T2: where three ice streams flow together at Konkordiaplatz, the ice is about 900 m deep — nearly a kilometer of ice under your feet (teach: an ice confluence). T2/T3: a glacier isn't frozen still — it FLOWS downhill like an extremely slow river, and as it grinds along it gouges the classic U-shaped valleys and drops ridges of rubble called moraines at its edges (teach: glaciers as landscape sculptors — U-valley, moraine). T3/T4: the whole Jungfrau-Aletsch area is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a living record of how Ice Age glaciers shaped Europe's mountains — the Aletsch has already pulled back more than 3 km since the 1800s, leaving fresh bare rock and young 'pioneer' forest where the ice used to be (dinner-test candidate: you can read a glacier's retreat in the ground it left). T4/T5: meltwater from the Aletsch feeds the Rhone, and alpine glaciers like it act as Europe's 'water towers' — storing winter snow and releasing it through the dry summer to rivers that millions of people depend on.
source: Grokipedia: Aletsch Glacier (primary per pipeline). Wikipedia: Aletsch Glacier; Jungfrau-Aletsch protected area; Moraine; Konkordiaplatz. UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Swiss Alps Jungfrau-Aletsch, inscribed 2001).
framing_note: PLACE ladder adding alpine/temperate-glacier breadth beyond the poles; distractors are other alpine features and glaciers (the Rhone Glacier, the Mer de Glace, a cirque vs. a moraine, the Matterhorn vs. the Jungfrau). Accuracy rail: 'largest/longest glacier in the Alps' is the correct scope claim (not 'in Europe' — that title goes to Vatnajokull), and the length is shrinking, so give it as 'about 23 km / roughly 20 km today'. Dinner-test payoff: the glacier as a moving sculptor whose retreat you can read in the fresh rock and pioneer forest it leaves behind. Lane border: none — glacier landforms and hydrology are core geography.
